explanation:
## How Auction Draft Budgeting Works

In a standard fantasy football auction every manager gets the same budget — **$200 in most ESPN, Yahoo and Sleeper leagues** — and must fill every roster spot with a minimum bid of $1. That creates the core constraint:

```
Bench Reserve = bench spots × $ per bench spot (usually $1)
Starter Budget = Total Budget − Bench Reserve
Position Budget = Starter Budget × strategy %
```

With a 16-man roster (9 starters, 7 bench) and a $200 budget, you reserve $7 for the bench and work with **$193 for starters**.

## Position Splits by Strategy (% of starter budget)

| Position | Balanced | RB-heavy | Zero RB | Stars & Scrubs |
|----------|----------|----------|---------|----------------|
| QB | 8% | 6% | 8% | 5% |
| RB | 38% | 52% | 18% | 45% |
| WR | 38% | 28% | 56% | 40% |
| TE | 10% | 8% | 12% | 4% |
| DST | 3% | 3% | 3% | 3% |
| K | 3% | 3% | 3% | 3% |

## Worked Example — $200, Balanced, 7 Bench Spots

| Line | Math | Amount |
|------|------|--------|
| Bench reserve | 7 × $1 | $7 |
| Starter budget | $200 − $7 | $193 |
| QB | 8% × $193 | $15 |
| RB | 38% × $193 | $73 |
| WR | 38% × $193 | $73 |
| TE | 10% × $193 | $19 |
| DST | 3% × $193 | $6 |
| K | remainder | $7 |

That RB/WR pool of ~$146 typically buys **two top-15 players (~$45-$60 each) plus two mid-tier starters (~$15-$25 each)**.

## Strategy Notes

- **Balanced:** safest for first-time auction drafters; you stay live on every nomination.
- **RB-heavy (Hero RB):** land 1-2 elite backs early; works best in leagues that start 2 RB + FLEX.
- **Zero RB:** punt on expensive backs, dominate WR, buy RB volume late at $1-$8 each.
- **Stars and Scrubs:** 60-70% of your budget on 2-3 studs, then $1-$4 lottery tickets everywhere else. Highest ceiling, thinnest margin for injury.

## Auction-Day Rules of Thumb

- **Never end with money left over.** $10 unspent is a starter you didn't buy.
- **Nominate players you don't want** early — drain rivals' budgets while prices run hot.
- **Prices fall late.** The first 10 players sold usually go 10-20% over fair value; patience buys discounts.
- **Track inflation:** if managers overpay early, your remaining dollars are worth more — adjust your max bids up.
- **$1 kicker and DST, always.** Streaming them in-season costs nothing.

faq.q: How much money do you get in a fantasy football auction draft?
faq.a: The standard auction budget is $200 per team on ESPN, Yahoo and Sleeper, though leagues can customize it ($100, $300, even $1,000). The amount itself doesn't matter — value is relative, so a $60 running back in a $200 league is the same as a $30 back in a $100 league. Every roster spot must be filled with a minimum bid of $1.

faq.q: How should I split a $200 auction budget by position?
faq.a: A balanced split with 7 bench spots reserves $7 for the bench and spends the $193 remainder roughly as: QB $15 (8%), RB $73 (38%), WR $73 (38%), TE $19 (10%), DST $6 and K $7. RB and WR together should absorb 70-80% of your starter money in most formats, because that's where weekly scoring separation lives.

faq.q: How much should I spend on my bench in an auction draft?
faq.a: As little as possible — $1 per bench spot is the standard plan, so a 7-man bench costs $7 (3.5% of a $200 budget). Bench players are replaceable via waivers all season; starters are not. Some managers reserve $2-$3 per spot to win late bidding on high-upside handcuffs, but going beyond ~$15-$20 total on bench weakens your starting lineup.

faq.q: What is the Zero RB auction strategy?
faq.a: Zero RB means skipping expensive running backs entirely and loading up on elite wide receivers, who historically get injured less and bust less often. In auction terms that's roughly 56% of starter money on WR and only ~18% on RB, buying volume backs late for $1-$8 each. It works best in PPR formats with 3 WR starting slots.

Stars and Scrubs concentrates 60-70% of your budget on 2-3 elite players — say $65 + $55 + $45 = $165 of a $200 budget — then fills the rest of the roster with $1-$4 players. It has the highest ceiling of any auction strategy because elite players win weeks, but one injury to a stud can sink the season, so it suits managers who work the waiver wire hard.

faq.q: How much should I pay for a quarterback in an auction?
faq.a: In 1-QB leagues, plan on 5-8% of your starter budget — about $10-$16 in a $200 league. Elite QBs (Allen, Jackson tier) go for $25-$35, but the position is deep: the QB8-QB12 range routinely costs under $10 and scores within 3-4 points per week of the elites. In Superflex or 2-QB leagues, double or triple that allocation — QBs become the most expensive position.

faq.q: When is the best time to do a 2026 fantasy football auction draft?
faq.a: The sweet spot is the two weeks between the third preseason week and the NFL 2026 season kickoff on Thursday, September 10, 2026. Drafting after final roster cuts (early September) means you draft with real depth charts and avoid burning auction dollars on players who get cut or lose their starting job in camp.

faq.q: Should I spend my whole budget in an auction draft?
faq.a: Yes — ending the auction with unspent money is pure waste, since leftover dollars have zero value once drafting ends. The goal is to end with exactly $0 remaining beyond the $1 minimums you still owe for unfilled spots. If you find yourself with surplus cash late, raise your max bids on remaining targets: late-auction players routinely sell below fair value.

faq.q: What is auction inflation and how do I use it?
faq.a: Inflation happens when managers overpay early: if the room spends 20% over projected values on the first 15 players sold, the money left in the room is chasing fewer good players, so remaining stars sell for more — and late-round values sell for less. Track total money spent vs total projected value spent; if the ratio is above 1, bump your max bids on elite targets and expect bargains at the end.

faq.q: Does this calculator work for budgets other than $200?
faq.a: Yes. Enter any budget — $100, $260, $1,000 — and the calculator scales the bench reserve and position splits proportionally. The strategy percentages stay the same because auction value is relative: what matters is the share of total money each position gets, not the absolute dollar amounts.

example.title: Example: $200 balanced auction budget with 7 bench spots
steps: **Bench reserve**: 7 bench spots x $1 minimum bid = $7 set aside.
**Starter budget**: $200 - $7 = $193 to spend on your 9 starters.
**Position split (Balanced)**: QB 8% = $15, RB 38% = $73, WR 38% = $73, TE 10% = $19, DST 3% = $6, K = $7 (remainder).
**Sanity check**: $15 + $73 + $73 + $19 + $6 + $7 = $193, plus the $7 bench = the full $200.
